'''Alexander McAulay''' (9 November 1863 – 5 July 1931) was a mathematician and physicist who was the first professor of mathematics and physics at the [[University of Tasmania]], [[Hobart]], Australia.<ref name=ADB_7293>{{Cite Australian Dictionary of Biography |first=Scott |last=Bruce |title=Alexander McAulay (1863–1931) |volume=10 |year=1986 |id2=mcaulay-alexander-7293 |access-date=19 December 2025}}</ref> He was also a proponent of [[dual quaternion]]s, which he termed "octonions" or "Clifford biquaternions".

== Life ==
McAulay was born on 9 November 1863 and attended [[Kingswood School]] in Bath. He proceeded to [[Caius College, Cambridge]], there taking up a study of the [[quaternion]] algebra. In 1883 he published an article "Some general theorems in quaternion integration".<ref>A. McAulay (1883) [[Messenger of Mathematics]] 13:26 to 37</ref> McAulay took his degree in 1886,<ref>{{acad|id=FML883A|name=McAulay, Alexander}}</ref> and began to reflect on the instruction of students in quaternion theory. In an article "Establishment of the fundamental properties of quaternions",<ref>McAulay (1888) ''Messenger of Mathematics'' 18:131 to 136</ref> he suggested improvements to the texts then in use. He also wrote a technical article<ref>A. McAulay (1888) "The transformation of multiple surface integrals into multiple line integrals", ''Messenger of Mathematics'' 18:139 to 45</ref> on [[Integration (mathematics)|integration]].

Departing for [[Australia]], he became a lecturer and tutor in mathematics at [[Ormond College, Melbourne|Ormond College]], University of Melbourne, from 1888 to 1895, being appointed first lecturer of mathematics in 1893.<ref name=ADB_7293 /> As a distant correspondent, he participated in a vigorous debate about the place of quaternions in [[physics education]].<ref>[[Michael J. Crowe]] (1967) [[A History of Vector Analysis]], U. Notre Dame Press. Chapter 6 details McAulay's four contributions in 1893 and 94 to the debate on vectors and quaternions.</ref> In 1893 his book ''Utility of Quaternions in Physics'' was published. [[A. S. Hathaway]] contributed a positive review<ref>[[A. S. Hathaway]] (1894) [https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1894-03-08/S0002-9904-1894-00201-8/S0002-9904-1894-00201-8.pdf Review: ''Utility of Quaternions in Physics''], [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] 3(8):179–85</ref> and [[Peter Guthrie Tait]] praised it in these terms:
{{Blockquote|text=Here, at last, we exclaim, is a man who has caught the full spirit of the quaternion system: the real ''aestus'', the ''awen'' of the Welsh Bards, the ''divinus [[afflatus]]'' that transports the poet beyond the limits of sublunary things! Intuitively recognizing its power, he snatches up the magnificent weapon which [[William Rowan Hamilton|Hamilton]] tenders us all, and at once dashes off to the jungle on the quest of big game.<ref>{{cite news | author=[[Peter Guthrie Tait]] | title=Quaternions as an Instrument in Physical Research | work=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | date=28 December 1893 | url=https://www.nature.com/articles/049193a0 | access-date=28 April 2024}}</ref>}}

In 1896, McAulay took up the position of first professor of mathematics and physics at the newly-founded [[University of Tasmania]]. He ceased teaching in 1924 due to incipient blindness and was selected as research professor until his retirement in 1929.<ref name=ADB_7293 />

Following [[William Kingdon Clifford]], who had extended quaternions to [[dual quaternion]]s, McAulay made a special study of this [[hypercomplex number]] system. In 1898 McAulay published, through [[Cambridge University Press]], his ''Octonions: a Development of Clifford's Biquaternions''.<ref>Rev N. M. Ferres (1895). [https://archive.org/details/philtrans00295009 Preview of ''Octonions'']. ''Proceedings of the Royal Society''. 59: 169, weblink from [[Archive.org]]</ref>

McAulay died from cerebral haemorrhage on 5 July 1931, in his home at [[Sandy Bay, Tasmania]], and was buried in Hobart.<ref name=ADB_7293 />

His brother [[Francis Sowerby Macaulay]], who stayed in England, also contributed to [[ring theory]]. The University of Tasmania has commemorated the McAulays' contributions in ''Winter Public Lectures''.<ref>[[University of Tasmania]]: [https://web.archive.org/web/20070613045353/http://www.phys.utas.edu.au/physics/AIP_TasBranch/program/McAulay_public_lectures.htm McAulay Public Lectures archived from 2007-06-13]</ref>
